campaign.name: The 60-Minute Project Squad
campaign.thesis: Final-year students do not lack AI hype — they lack one AI project they built themselves. Sell the finished project, not the webinar, and let students recruit their own squad.
campaign.coreMessage: One real AI project. 60 minutes. Free. Bring a friend.
campaign.objective: 500 completed registrations from final-year engineering students in 7 days with a total budget of ₹2,000 (target, not a forecast).
campaign.insight: In placement season every resume carries the same to-do app and weather app. Students have watched plenty of AI content but have shipped nothing with it, and they distrust 'another webinar' that ends in slides. They act on what a friend forwards, not on a poster.
campaign.differentiator: Instead of a poster, every registrant gets a personal Squad link and the campaign is built around forwarding in peer groups, where a friend's message carries more trust than an ad.

a.label: Outcome-led
a.subhead: Walk away with a working AI project you can demo in your next interview — built live, in one hour.

b.label: Barrier-led
b.subhead: Never built anything with AI? Start here: one guided hour, one project, zero slides-only theory.

hooks.hookA: Your resume has a to-do app. So does everyone else's. Add an AI project that actually runs.
hooks.hookB: You don't need to be an ML expert to build with AI. Build your first project in 60 minutes.

outcomesProposed: Understand how a simple AI-powered app is put together, end to end.
Build and run a small working AI project during the session.
Know how to describe the project and what you built in a resume or interview.

audience.name: Placement-pressured CS/IT final-years
audience.motivation: Stand out in interviews with a project that is not a tutorial clone.
audience.objection: 'Another webinar — I'll get slides and no output.'
audience.message: Leave with a project you can demo, not slides.
audience.channel: WhatsApp / Telegram class, hostel and placement groups

audience.name: Non-CS branch final-years (ECE/EEE/Mech/Civil)
audience.motivation: Want AI skills for broader job options but feel AI is 'for CS students'.
audience.objection: 'I don't know ML — this isn't for me.'
audience.message: You don't need to be an ML expert to build your first AI project.

audience.name: Club-connected connectors (coding / E-Cell / IEEE club members)
audience.motivation: Add value for their members and look useful to their community.
audience.objection: 'I don't want to spam my group with something low quality.'
audience.message: A free hands-on session you can forward, with a ready-to-send message.
audience.channel: Campus club & community admin outreach (LinkedIn/Instagram DMs, Discord)

channels.name: WhatsApp / Telegram peer groups
channels.why: Highest trust and zero media cost. Students act on a forward from a classmate. Distribution starts from my own network and spreads through the Squad link.
channels.fallback: If seeding stalls, post the message in open student Telegram/Discord communities and ask 10 friends in different colleges to forward once.

channels.name: Instagram Reels (organic + ₹1,200 boost)
channels.why: The only affordable way to reach students outside my network and non-CS branches; the boost doubles as the message experiment.
channels.fallback: If cost per visit is more than 2x the assumption by day 3, stop the boost and move the money to Squad prizes.

channels.name: Campus club & community outreach
channels.why: One admin forward reaches hundreds of members. Cold DMs cost nothing but time.
channels.fallback: Expect most DMs to be ignored. If under 5 of 40 admins reply by day 3, redirect effort to WhatsApp seeding.

supportingMechanism.name: Squad referral link
supportingMechanism.description: After registering, each student gets a personal link. Friends who register through it count toward their Squad. Top 5 referrers by verified, unique registrations receive a ₹100 reward.

rejectedChannels: Google / YouTube ads — CPC too high for ₹2,000; would buy < 100 clicks
LinkedIn ads — minimum budgets and CPM too high for this budget
Email — no list; cold email to students is spam
Printed posters — untrackable, needs college permission, slow
Paid influencers — a single post would consume the whole budget

funnel.difficultyNote: 500 is a stretch. It needs roughly 1,700 landing-page visits converting at about 29% with an active referral loop. With no existing audience, the realistic outcome is probably between the downside (about 100) and base (about 500) cases. The plan is built to learn fast which channel works, not to promise 500.

'Last 48 hours' message; release ₹300 reserve only if funnel is healthy.

experiments.name: Message hook test — career proof vs. no-barrier
experiments.hypothesis: A career-proof hook ('your resume has a to-do app') will generate more completed registrations per ₹100 than a no-barrier hook, because final-years are under placement pressure.
experiments.why: Message choice is the biggest uncertainty and the paid budget is too small to test it twice.
experiments.audience: Engineering students on Instagram (India, age 20–23); Instagram Reels boost.
experiments.variants: Hook A: "Your resume has a to-do app. So does everyone else's. Add an AI project that actually runs." vs Hook B: "You don't need to be an ML expert to build with AI. Build your first project in 60 minutes." Same reel format, same landing page, same budget (₹300 each).
experiments.independent: Hook text in the first 3 seconds and caption.
experiments.guardrail: Landing-page-to-registration conversion stays at or above 15% (so cheap clicks are not low-intent).
experiments.data: Instagram Ads Manager for spend and reach; the asset records utm_content=hookA|hookB on every visit and registration.
experiments.decision: Needs at least 25 landing visits per variant. Winner = at least 25% higher registrations per ₹100 with the guardrail met.
experiments.positive: Put the ₹600 scale budget behind the winner.
experiments.negative: If the other hook wins, switch to it and keep its wording for WhatsApp copy.
experiments.inconclusive: Split the ₹600 evenly and use both hooks for different segments (A for CS/IT, B for non-CS).

experiments.name: Landing page — outcome-led vs. barrier-led subhead and CTA
experiments.hypothesis: Barrier-led copy ('Start my first AI project') will lift visit-to-registration conversion by at least 5 percentage points because many visitors doubt they are 'ready'.
experiments.why: Every visitor passes through the page. A small conversion lift multiplies across all three channels.
experiments.variants: Variant A: outcome-led subhead + button 'Reserve my free seat'. Variant B: barrier-led subhead + button 'Start my first AI project'. Headline, form and layout are identical.
experiments.guardrail: Form-start-to-completion rate stays at or above 60% (the copy must not attract people who abandon the form).
experiments.data: Built into the asset: 50/50 random assignment (sticky per browser), events carry the variant. Read on the Dashboard.
experiments.duration: Days 1–5 or until 150 visits per variant, whichever is later.
experiments.decision: Low statistical power at this volume, so results are directional. Choose B if conversion is at least 5 points above A with 150+ visits each.
experiments.positive: Make variant B the default for all traffic.
experiments.inconclusive: Keep A and test the form length (name + email only) instead.

experiments.name: Peer referral — personal Squad link vs. ordinary share
experiments.hypothesis: Registrants who get a personal Squad link with progress and a reward will bring at least 1.5x more referred registrations per registrant than registrants shown a generic share link.
experiments.why: The plan depends on the referral loop contributing roughly 30% of registrations. If it does not, the 500 target is unreachable.
experiments.variants: Control: generic 'share with a friend' link and message. Treatment: personal link, Squad progress (target: 3 friends), and note about the top-5 ₹100 rewards. Randomized 50/50 per registrant.
experiments.independent: Type of share prompt (generic vs. personal Squad link with progress and reward). Note: reward and personal link are bundled in the treatment.
experiments.primary: Referred registrations per registrant, by arm.
experiments.guardrail: Duplicate or invalid registrations stay below 10% of referred sign-ups (to catch gaming of rewards).
experiments.data: Built into the asset: the share arm is stored at registration and carried in the share link (arm=c / arm=t, plus ref code). Read on the Dashboard.
experiments.duration: Days 2–7 (each registrant has a 48-hour attribution window).
experiments.decision: Needs at least 100 registrants per arm. Treatment wins if referred registrations per registrant are at least 1.5x control and at least 0.15 absolute.
experiments.positive: Show the Squad link to everyone and increase the reward share of the budget.
experiments.negative: Drop rewards, keep the simple share button and move the ₹500 to the boost.
experiments.inconclusive: Run a follow-up isolating reward vs. personal link.

definitions.reach: People who could see a message (impressions or group members). Estimated; not tracked by the asset.
definitions.visits: Landing-page visits recorded by the asset (page_view).
definitions.registrations: Completed registrations (registration_completed) with a valid, unique email.
definitions.attendance: People who join the live session. Not measured by the asset; read from the webinar tool after the event.
